title: Radical politics, conservative taste in music
summary: John notes the contrast between Rose's revolutionary socialism and his preference for preserving true New Orleans jazz.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live

blocks.x: It seems, Al, that socially and politically, we haven't really talked about your political views yet, but you say that you're a revolutionary socialist.
Yeah, I think that's a fair estimate.

And I'd like to ask you a little bit about that. But you tend to be, it seems that you tend to be extremely, I don't know whether the word radical would be correct, in your political views and extremely conservative in your views of music. That is, when all the figures musically that have been either used or in some way reflect a social change, these musicians don't appeal to you at all. The musicians that appeal to you are the ones that reflect a society that might have been slower, more static. I'm thinking of early 19th century New Orleans. That you're interested in the preservation of a true, what you call a true New Orleans form of music. And that you're not very interested in whether this music changes into another kind of form. In fact, you don't believe in any evolutionary views in this sense. Well, I believe that the jazz has gone through its process of evolution and died. All right. All right. But you're interested in that true form.

So that the question of how, what new musical form may arise on the horizon doesn't interest you very much right now, because it's all speculation or it's all, it doesn't, it just hasn't come into existence yet. That's right. But politically, you seem to be very interested in change taking place in the culture. And maybe, I just wonder how you roll out.
